name: Quinbolone

lead: Quinbolone is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid developed by Parke-Davis and first described in 1962. It is a prodrug: after swallowing, the body converts it to boldenone, which carries most of the effect.[1]

The appearance link is muscle growth and body composition, the purpose for which anabolic steroids are used. It was a commercial failure and is little used, with limited illicit use in bodybuilding.[1]

paras: It was taken by mouth and, unlike many oral steroids, lacks the 17-alpha-alkyl group associated with liver toxicity.[1] Mid-1960s Italian clinical studies examined it as an anabolic agent and looked at liver function.[2][3] Later reports covered its use in anemia in dialysis patients.[6]

As a boldenone prodrug it may produce androgenic effects and some conversion to estrogens.[1] It is a Schedule III substance in the US and Schedule IV in Canada, and it is banned in most competitive sports; its metabolites are detectable in tests.[1] A 1980 study found it ineffective for preventing hereditary angioedema attacks, unlike 17-alpha-alkylated steroids.[5]

chain: More muscle mass (the aim of anabolic steroids)
angle.text: Quinbolone was developed as an anabolic agent; studies measured nitrogen metabolism and clinical response. It is now of mainly historical interest.

lead: Quinbolone is an androstane anabolic-androgenic steroid, chemically the cyclopentenyl enol ether of boldenone, which acts as a prodrug of boldenone when taken orally.[1] It was sold in Italy under the names Anabolicum and Anabolvis.[1]

It was developed by Parke-Davis as an orally active steroid with little or no liver toxicity and was first described in 1962. Because of the high doses needed, cost and inconvenience, it was commercially unsuccessful and other steroids filled its uses.[1] Its illicit use in bodybuilding and athletics appears limited.[1]
Published research is mainly Italian clinical work from the 1960s and 1970s on anabolic effects, nitrogen balance, hormone excretion, liver function and use in dialysis anemia.[2][3][4][5][6][7]
infobox: US Schedule III; Canada Schedule IV

paras: Quinbolone is largely inactive itself and is converted to boldenone, with some boldenone further converted to estrogens.[1] A 1971 study examined the metabolism of quinbolone and related 1-dehydroandrostanes in humans.[8]
Marketed in Italy, it never achieved wide commercial success.[1] It is a controlled substance in the US and Canada and is prohibited in most sports.[1]

Italian clinical studies from 1965 evaluated quinbolone as a new anabolic preparation and examined liver function and urinary steroid excretion.[2][3][7] A 1967 study looked at its action on nitrogen metabolism,[6] a 1977 report on pituitary activity,[4] and a 1980 study on anemia in uremic patients on hemodialysis.[5] A comparison of androgens for hereditary angioedema found quinbolone, nandrolone and mesterolone ineffective compared with danazol and stanozolol.[9]
